claim: Two-photon (2P) fluorescence imaging through gradient index (GRIN) lens-based endoscopes is fundamental to investigate the functional properties of neural populations in deep brain circuits.

claim: GRIN lenses have intrinsic optical aberrations, which severely degrade their imaging performance.
source: However, GRIN lenses have intrinsic optical aberrations, which severely degrade their imaging performance.

claim: GRIN aberrations decrease the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and spatial resolution of fluorescence signals, especially in lateral portions of the field-of-view (FOV).
source: GRIN aberrations decrease the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and spatial resolution of fluorescence signals, especially in lateral portions of the field-of-view (FOV), leading to restricted FOV and smaller number of recorded neurons.
evidence: This is supported by citations and experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: GRIN aberrations lead to restricted FOV and smaller number of recorded neurons.

claim: GRIN aberrations are especially relevant for GRIN lenses of several millimeters in length, which are needed to reach the deeper regions of the rodent brain.

claim: Long corrected microendoscopes had improved spatial resolution, enabling imaging in significantly enlarged FOVs.
source: Long corrected microendoscopes had improved spatial resolution, enabling imaging in significantly enlarged FOVs.

claim: Long corrected microendoscopes are powerful new tools enabling population imaging with unprecedented large FOV and high spatial resolution in the most ventral regions of the mouse brain.
source: Long corrected microendoscopes are powerful new tools enabling population imaging with unprecedented large FOV and high spatial resolution in the most ventral regions of the mouse brain.

claim: Deep ventral regions of the brain, such as the olfactory cortex, the hypothalamus, and the amygdala play fundamental roles in controlling the processing of sensory information (Endo and Kazama, 2022), circadian rhythms (Sternson, 2013), hormone release (Sternson, 2013), decision making (Phelps et al., 2014), and adaptation of instinctive and motivational behavior (Phelps et al., 2014).

claim: Imaging deep ventral brain regions typically requires the use of light guides, which relay the focal plane of the microscope objective down to the target brain area.

source: Other ventral brain regions, such as the olfactory cortex, can be imaged with an invasive preparation, which does not require a GRIN lens, but which is incompatible with imaging in awake behaving animals (Roland et al., 2017; Pashkovski et al., 2020).

source: One limitation of GRIN lens-based endoscopy is that GRIN lenses suffer from intrinsic optical aberrations (Bortoletto et al., 2011; Lee and Yun, 2011).

claim: GRIN aberrations distort the point spread function (PSF) and enlarge the excitation volume of the focal spot, leading to reduced SNR of fluorescence signals and decreased spatial resolution (Antonini et al., 2020; Wang and Ji, 2012; Wang and Ji, 2013).
source: GRIN aberrations distort the point spread function (PSF) and enlarge the excitation volume of the focal spot, leading to reduced SNR of fluorescence signals and decreased spatial resolution (Antonini et al., 2020; Wang and Ji, 2012; Wang and Ji, 2013).

claim: The effect of GRIN aberrations is not uniform across the FOV and is particularly relevant in lateral portions of the FOV, generating uneven spatial resolution and inhomogeneous amplitude of fluorescence signals across the FOV (Antonini et al., 2020; Wang and Ji, 2012; Wang and Ji, 2013).
source: This effect is not uniform across the FOV and is particularly relevant in lateral portions of the FOV, generating uneven spatial resolution and inhomogeneous amplitude of fluorescence signals across the FOV (Antonini et al., 2020; Wang and Ji, 2012; Wang and Ji, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Previous studies using 2P imaging through GRIN lenses in ventral regions of the mouse brain were limited to imaging a small number of neurons with uneven spatial resolution across the FOV and low SNR in lateral portion of the FOV (Jennings et al., 2019; Jung et al., 2022; Piantadosi et al., 2024).
source: As a consequence of these limitations, previous studies using 2P imaging through GRIN lenses in ventral regions of the mouse brain were limited to imaging a small number of neurons with uneven spatial resolution across the FOV and low SNR in lateral portion of the FOV (Jennings et al., 2019; Jung et al., 2022; Piantadosi et al., 2024).

source: Alternatively, adaptive optics through pupil segmentation was used to efficiently correct GRIN aberrations, increasing the intensity of recorded fluorescence signals and enlarging the imaging FOV (Wang and Ji, 2012; Wang and Ji, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

source: Recently, a novel method based on 3D microprinting of polymer optics was developed to correct for GRIN aberrations by placing specifically designed aspherical corrective lenses at the back end of the GRIN lens (Antonini et al., 2020).

claim: The 3D microprinting approach is attractive because it is built-in on the GRIN lens and corrected microendoscopes are ready-to-use, requiring no change in the optical set-up.
source: This approach is attractive because it is built-in on the GRIN lens and corrected microendoscopes are ready-to-use, requiring no change in the optical set-up.

claim: Two GRIN singlet rod lenses suitable for multiphoton fluorescence imaging in ventral regions of the mouse brain were selected with NA = 0.5 on both sides, 500 µm diameter, 1.5 and 2.0 pitch, and 6.4 mm and 8.8 mm length, respectively.
source: We selected two GRIN singlet rod lenses (hereon GRIN rods) suitable for multiphoton fluorescence imaging in ventral regions of the mouse brain. The two selected GRIN rods had NA = 0.5 on both sides, 500 µm diameter, 1.5 and 2.0 pitch, and 6.4 mm and 8.8 mm length, respectively.
evidence: This describes the materials used in the study.

claim: For both GRIN rods, an optical assembly was modeled composed of the GRIN rod, a thin layer of glass (representing a 100-µm-thick glass coverslip) attached to the back end of the GRIN rod, and an aspheric corrective lens aligned to the rod and attached to the opposite side of the glass coverslip with respect to the GRIN rod.
source: For both GRIN rods, we modeled an optical assembly composed of the GRIN rod, a thin layer of glass (representing a 100-µm-thick glass coverslip) attached to the back end of the GRIN rod, and an aspheric corrective lens (here on called corrective lens) aligned to the rod and attached to the opposite side of the glass coverslip with respect to the GRIN rod (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This describes the design of the optical assembly, supported by Figure 1A and B.

claim: The design of the corrective lens was an iterative process in which the parameters that define the corrective lens surface were automatically varied to obtain the highest and most homogeneous spatial resolution possible over the longest possible radial distance from the optical axis.
source: The design of the corrective lens was an iterative process in which the parameters that define the corrective lens surface were automatically varied to obtain the highest and most homogeneous spatial resolution possible over the longest possible radial distance from the optical axis (see Supplementary file 1 and Materials and methods for details on simulation parameters).
evidence: This describes the optimization process used in the design.

claim: The corrective lens profile was simulated such that the Strehl ratio of the corrected microendoscope remained above the threshold of 0.8 for the longest possible radial distance from the optical axis.
source: More specifically, we simulated the corrective lens profile such that the Strehl ratio (defined as the peak intensity of the focal spot of an aberrated optical system normalized to the peak intensity of the focal spot of the ideal optical system, Smith, 2008) of the corrected microendoscope remained above the threshold of 0.8 for the longest possible radial distance from the optical axis.
evidence: This describes the optimization criterion used in the design.

claim: The values of Strehl ratio equal to 0.8 corresponded to the lower bound of the diffraction-limited condition set by the Maréchal criterion (Antonini et al., 2020; Smith, 2008).
source: The values of Strehl ratio equal to 0.8 corresponded to the lower bound of the diffraction-limited condition set by the Maréchal criterion (Antonini et al., 2020; Smith, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Simulations showed that the profiles of the two corrective lenses displayed in Figure 1A and B led to an increase in the radius of the diffraction-limited FOV compared to the case in which the corrective lens was not positioned in the back end of the GRIN rods (uncorrected microendoscopes).
source: Our simulations showed that the profiles of the two corrective lenses displayed in Figure 1A and B led to an increase in the radius of the diffraction-limited FOV compared to the case in which the corrective lens was not positioned in the back end of the GRIN rods (uncorrected microendoscopes).
evidence: This is a finding from simulations, supported by Figure 1A and B.

claim: The profile of the corrective optical element was specific to the type of GRIN rod considered.
source: The profile of the corrective optical element was specific to the type of GRIN rod considered.
evidence: This is a finding from the design process, supported by the data.

claim: The simulated increase in the radius of the diffraction-limited FOV was 3.50 times and 3.35 times for the 6.4 mm-long and 8.8 mm-long probe, respectively.
source: The simulated increase in the radius of the diffraction-limited FOV was 3.50 times and 3.35 times for the 6.4 mm-long and 8.8 mm-long probe, respectively (Figure 1C and E).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from simulations, supported by Figure 1C and E.

claim: All simulations were performed maximizing aberration correction in the simulated focal plane of the microendoscopes.
source: All simulations were performed maximizing aberration correction in the simulated focal plane of the microendoscopes (imaging plane in Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This describes the simulation conditions.

claim: In corrected microendoscopes, for off-axis rays (radial distance from the optical axis >40 μm) the Strehl ratio was >0.8 (Maréchal criterion) in a larger volume compared to uncorrected microendoscopes.
source: In corrected microendoscopes, we found that for off-axis rays (radial distance from the optical axis >40 μm) the Strehl ratio was >0.8 (Maréchal criterion) in a larger volume compared to uncorrected microendoscopes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), demonstrating that the aberration correction method developed in this study extends for short distances beyond the simulated focal plane.
evidence: This is a finding from simulations, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: At a radial distance of ~90 μm from the optical axis, the axial range in which the Strehl ratio was >0.8 in corrected microendoscopes was 28 μm and 19 μm for the 6.4 mm-long and the 8.8 mm-long microendoscope, respectively.
source: For example, at a radial distance of ~90 μm from the optical axis, the axial range in which the Strehl ratio was >0.8 in corrected microendoscopes was 28 μm and 19 μm for the 6.4 mm-long and the 8.8 mm-long microendoscope, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from simulations.

claim: Decentering the optical axis of the corrective lens from the optical axis of the GRIN rod rapidly disrupted the optical properties of the corrected microendoscopes.
source: Decentering the optical axis of the corrective lens from the optical axis of the GRIN rod rapidly disrupted the optical properties of the corrected microendoscopes (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from simulations, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: For both the 6.4 mm-long and 8.8 mm-long GRIN rods, the PSF of the uncorrected probe was strongly aberrated and highly irregular at ~90 µm away from the center of the FOV.
source: For both the 6.4 mm-long and 8.8 mm-long GRIN rods, we found that the PSF of the uncorrected probe was strongly aberrated and highly irregular at ~90 µm away from the center of the FOV (Figure 1D and F).
evidence: This is a finding from simulations, supported by Figure 1D and F.

claim: In the corrected microendoscopes the PSF had regular shape and, at >90 µm away from the optical axis, it was similar to the one measured at the center of the FOV.
source: In contrast, in the corrected microendoscopes the PSF had regular shape and, at >90 µm away from the optical axis, it was similar to the one measured at the center of the FOV (Figure 1D and F, see also Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a finding from simulations, supported by Figure 1D and F.

claim: 3D microprinting based on 2P lithography was used to fabricate aspherical corrective lens prototypes.
source: Due to the small size of the simulated corrective lenses (diameter: 500 µm; height: few tens of µm), we first used 3D microprinting based on 2P lithography to fabricate aspherical corrective lens prototypes (Figure 2A and B; Liberale et al., 2010; Gonzalez‐Hernandez et al., 2023).
evidence: This describes the fabrication method, supported by Figure 2A and B and citations.

claim: The prototypes were replicated using a molding procedure.
source: We then replicated the prototypes using a molding procedure (Schaap and Bellouard, 2013; Figure 2C).
evidence: This describes the replication method, supported by Figure 2C and citation.

claim: The molding strategy enabled obtaining large numbers of aspherical lens replica directly manufactured onto round glass coverslips in a much faster and cheaper way compared to 3D microprinting.
source: The molding strategy enabled us to obtain large numbers of aspherical lens replica directly manufactured onto round glass coverslips in a much faster and cheaper way compared to 3D microprinting.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of the molding method, supported by logical inference.

claim: Strong off-axis aberrations of the GRIN lens generated a significant loss of fluorescence intensity in the marginal portions of the FOV in uncorrected microendoscopes.
source: Strong off-axis aberrations of the GRIN lens generated a significant loss of fluorescence intensity in the marginal portions of the FOV in uncorrected microendoscopes (for both the 6.4 mm-long, Figure 3A and B, and the 8.8 mm-long, Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is an experimental finding, supported by Figure 3A-D.

claim: Fluorescence signal was collected over longer distances from the center of the FOV in corrected microendoscopes.
source: In contrast, fluorescence signal was collected over longer distances from the center of the FOV in corrected microendoscopes (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This is an experimental finding, supported by Figure 3A-D.

claim: For GRIN rods of both lengths the full width at half maximum (FWHM) of the film profile obtained with uncorrected microendoscopes increased with distance from the optical axis and became rapidly larger than 20 µm.
source: Moreover, for GRIN rods of both lengths the full width at half maximum (FWHM) of the film profile obtained with uncorrected microendoscopes increased with distance from the optical axis and became rapidly larger than 20 µm.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the fluorescent film measurements.

claim: The film profile obtained with corrected microendoscopes showed more homogenous FWHM values across an extended FOV.
source: In contrast, the film profile obtained with corrected microendoscopes showed more homogenous FWHM values across an extended FOV (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This is an experimental finding, supported by Figure 3A-D.

claim: A relative increase of the effective FOV radius of 2.17 and 1.53 for the 6.4 mm-long and the 8.8 mm-long microendoscope, respectively, was observed.
source: We observed a relative increase of the effective FOV radius of 2.17 and 1.53 for the 6.4 mm-long and the 8.8 mm-long microendoscope, respectively (Table 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental finding, supported by Table 1.

claim: The enlargement of the effective FOV area was 4.7 times and 2.3 times for the 6.4 mm-long microendoscope and the 8.8 mm-long microendoscope, respectively.
source: This corresponded to an enlargement of the effective FOV area of 4.7 times and 2.3 times for the 6.4 mm-long microendoscope and the 8.8 mm-long microendoscope, respectively (Table 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental finding, supported by Table 1.

claim: These findings were in agreement with the results of the ray-trace simulations and the measurement of the subresolved fluorescence layers.
source: These findings were in agreement with the results of the ray-trace simulations (Figure 1) and the measurement of the subresolved fluorescence layers (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This is a statement comparing experimental and simulation results.

claim: Aberration correction enabled to clearly resolve neuronal somata and processes in the lateral portions of the FOV.
source: We found that aberration correction enabled to clearly resolve neuronal somata and processes in the lateral portions of the FOV, whereas in the absence of the corrective lens the same structures located in the peripheral portion of the FOV appeared dim, strongly aberrated, and hardly detectable (Figure 4, see also Figure 4—figure supplement 1 for an alternative visualization in which the FOVs of corrected microendoscopes are rescaled to match the real pixel size of the FOVs of uncorrected microendoscopes in the center of the image).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from imaging brain slices, supported by Figure 4.

claim: In the absence of the corrective lens the same structures located in the peripheral portion of the FOV appeared dim, strongly aberrated, and hardly detectable.
source: We found that aberration correction enabled to clearly resolve neuronal somata and processes in the lateral portions of the FOV, whereas in the absence of the corrective lens the same structures located in the peripheral portion of the FOV appeared dim, strongly aberrated, and hardly detectable (Figure 4, see also Figure 4—figure supplement 1 for an alternative visualization in which the FOVs of corrected microendoscopes are rescaled to match the real pixel size of the FOVs of uncorrected microendoscopes in the center of the image).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from imaging brain slices, supported by Figure 4.

claim: Simulated neurons had 3D distribution and anatomical properties (i.e. cell size and cell density) similar to those measured in the mouse olfactory cortex (Suzuki and Bekkers, 2010; Suzuki and Bekkers, 2011).
source: To build synthetic calcium data, we first generated neurons with 3D distribution and anatomical properties (i.e. cell size and cell density) similar to those measured in the mouse olfactory cortex (Suzuki and Bekkers, 2010; Suzuki and Bekkers, 2011), the ventral brain region which we will be imaging in vivo (see next section of Results), and the biophysical characteristics of one of the two indicators used in our experiments, jGCaMP8f (Zhang et al., 2023; see also Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the simulation parameters, supported by citations.

claim: The use of corrected probes allowed segmenting more ROIs with high SNR compared to uncorrected microendoscopes, shifting the distribution of SNR across ROIs to higher mean SNR values.
source: We found that the use of corrected probes allowed segmenting more ROIs with high SNR compared to uncorrected microendoscopes, shifting the distribution of SNR across ROIs to higher mean SNR values. This was true for both the microendoscopes based on the 6.4 mm-long GRIN rod (Figure 5B) and the microendoscope based on the 8.8 mm-long GRIN rod (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a finding from simulated data analysis, supported by Figure 5B and E.

claim: For both microendoscope types, aberration correction increased the maximal radial distance at which ROIs with high (>15) SNR could be observed.
source: Moreover, for both microendoscope types, aberration correction increased the maximal radial distance at which ROIs with high (>15) SNR could be observed (Figure 5C and F).
evidence: This is a finding from simulated data analysis, supported by Figure 5C and F.

claim: Correcting for optical aberrations increases the probability of recording ROIs with larger SNR of fluorescent signals.
source: These findings demonstrate that correcting for optical aberrations increases the probability of recording ROIs with larger SNR of fluorescent signals.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulated data analysis.

claim: Compared to uncorrected probes, corrected microendoscopes of both lengths led to lower fraction of pairs of adjacent cells whose activity correlated significantly more than expected.
